problem_motivation.content: Controlling defect creation is needed to conclusively link specific defects to emission spectra.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: but in order to conclusively correlate specific defects to their spectra, having control over the defect creation mechanism is required

problem_motivation.content: No satisfactory direct correlation between defect structures and quantum emission properties has yet been established.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: so far no satisfactory direct correlation between the defect structures and quantum emission properties has been established

problem_motivation.content: A more effective defect-generation method is needed for large-scale applications.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: For large-scale applications, a method to generate defects more effectively would be necessary.

problem_motivation.content: Whether those electron-irradiation effects also matter for ultra-low-energy singly charged ion irradiation is unclear.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Whether these effects play a role also for ultra-low-energy singly-charged ion irradiation of hBN remains unclear.

problem_motivation.content: More work is needed to understand hBN defect-engineering mechanisms experimentally and computationally
problem_motivation.evidence_span: more research is needed both experimentally and computationally to fully understand the mechanisms involved in the defect-engineering of hBN.

prior_approach.content: Different irradiation methods have been used to create quantum emitters in hBN.
prior_approach.evidence_span: It has already been shown that different kinds of irradiation can be used to create quantum emitters in hBN, including lasers [19], ions [20], neutrons [21] and electrons [11, 22].

prior_approach.content: Electron irradiation in STEM is one existing defect-generation method.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Electron irradiation, particularly in scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)

prior_approach.content: High-energy ion irradiation is another existing approach.
prior_approach.evidence_span: while high-energy ion irradiation

prior_approach.content: Analytical-potential molecular dynamics predicted high defect-creation efficiency for low-energy noble-gas ions.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Analytical potential molecular dynamics simulations have shown that low-energy noble-gas ions should have high defect creation efficiencies.

prior_approach.content: Prior simulations predicted best selectivity below 200 eV, with nitrogen single vacancies most prominent for heavier noble gases.
prior_approach.evidence_span: According to simulations with a potential benchmarked against density functional theory (DFT) [27], the best selectivity should be achievable at ion energies lower than 200 eV, where nitrogen single vacancies were reported to be the most prominent defect with noble gas projectiles heavier than Ne.

prior_approach.content: Lehtinen et al. predicted about 0.8 defects per 100 eV Ar ion with similar single-vacancy probabilities and higher double-vacancy probability.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In an earlier work, Lehtinen et al. [28] predicted that about 0.8 defects are created per 100 eV Ar ion with roughly equal probabilities (∼0.2) for creating boron (VB ) and nitrogen single vacancies (VN ) and roughly twice that for double vacancies (VBN ) in monolayer hBN.

prior_approach.content: Ghaderzadeh et al. predicted about 0.2 defects per 150 eV Ar ion and more VN than VBN or VB.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Ghaderzadeh et al. [27], on the other hand, reported about 0.2 defects being created per 150 eV Ar ion at low fluences. They predict a higher density of VN (∼0.4) than for VBN (∼0.3) and VB (∼0.2).

prior_approach.content: Electron irradiation experiments showed boron is more likely displaced than nitrogen at intermediate electron energies.
prior_approach.evidence_span: For electron irradiation, it was experimentally shown that intermediate electron energies (60–100 keV) are more likely to displace boron than nitrogen [23].

prior_approach.content: Electron irradiation in low-pressure oxygen preferentially removes boron from pore edges.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Electron irradiation in a low-pressure oxygen atmosphere has also been shown to result in preferential removal of boron, at least from pore edges [24], often leading to nitrogen-terminated pores.

prior_approach.content: Recent atomic-level (S)TEM studies of ion-induced hBN defects found mainly point defects.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Recent reports of atomic-level (S)TEM characterisation of ion-induced defects in hBN for mono- [29] and multilayers [25], find predominantly point defects being created.

prior_approach.content: Byrne et al. used 25 keV He+ irradiation and TEM imaging, measuring defect density and baseline density.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Byrne et al. [29] used 25 keV He+ ions with a fluence of 75 ions nm−2 , and found a defect density of 0.16 nm−2 , with 80 kV TEM imaging at a dose rate ranging from 500 to 700 e− /Å2 /s. Without irradiation, a baseline defect density of 0.03 nm−2 was measured.

prior_approach.content: Liang et al. used 500 keV He+ on multilayer hBN and found mostly boron single vacancies and impurity substitutions.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Liang et al. [25] used 500 keV He+ with a fluence of 30 ions nm−2 on multilayer hBN and measured a total of 0.08 defects nm−2 with high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM imaging at 80 kV, which were predominately boron single vacancies and its substitutions by impurity atoms.

prior_approach.content: Wang et al. characterized defects in exfoliated monolayer hBN without ion irradiation.
prior_approach.evidence_span: A study conducted by Wang et al. [30] characterized defects in exfoliated monolayer hBN at the atomic scale; however, no ion irradiation was conducted here.

prior_approach.content: The only direct prior experimental comparison to low-energy ion-irradiation simulations was in Refs. 31 and 32.
prior_approach.evidence_span: So far the only direct experimental comparison to the simulation studies [27, 28] for low-energy ion irradiation of monolayer hBN was carried out in Refs. [31, 32].

prior_approach.content: Similar ion-irradiation experiments on graphene primarily produced double vacancies with much less impurity filling.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Similar ion irradiation experiments conducted on graphene [35, 36] yielded primarily double vacancies and much lower vacancy filling by impurity atoms

prior_approach.content: Electron irradiation during imaging is a known source of hBN defects
prior_approach.evidence_span: Since electron irradiation during imaging is known to introduce defects into hBN [47–49], even under ultra-high vacuum and at an acceleration voltage of 60 kV [23, 50, 51]

prior_approach.content: Known contamination atoms can migrate on 2D materials and fill vacancies
prior_approach.evidence_span: Carbon and silicon atoms from the ubiquitous contamination, possibly mobilised during irradiation, are known to migrate on the surface of 2D materials and fill vacancies [52], especially at elevated temperatures [53].

prior_approach.content: Wang et al. reported high intrinsic defect density dominated by boron vacancies
prior_approach.evidence_span: Wang et al. [30] report a surprisingly high intrinsic defect density of 0.14 nm−2 where VB accounts for 78.7% of all the defects measured.

prior_approach.content: Liang et al. used 500 keV He+ irradiation of multilayer hBN dominated by electronic stopping
prior_approach.evidence_span: Liang et al. [25] irradiate multilayer hBN with 500 keV He+ ions where the interaction is dominated by inelastic effects (electronic stopping).

prior_approach.content: Byrne et al. irradiated monolayer hBN with 25 keV He+ and Ne+ and reported defect densities
prior_approach.evidence_span: Byrne et al. [29] irradiated monolayer hBN with He+ and Ne+ at 25 keV with different doses and report defect densities but no defect-type distribution.

prior_approach.content: Prior theory predicted 75–80% defect creation with similar probabilities for B and N single vacancies and many double vacancies under ~100 eV Ar
prior_approach.evidence_span: it was found, depending on the potential used, that an impinging Ar ion (≈ 100 eV) has a 75–80% chance to create a defect with the probability for creating a boron or nitrogen single vacancy being 17–20% each and about 40% for a double vacancy [28].

prior_approach.content: Another prior theory predicted about twice as many nitrogen vacancies as boron vacancies or double vacancies under 150 eV Ar
prior_approach.evidence_span: Another study used 150 eV Ar irradiation and predicted it should create roughly twice as many N single vacancies than B single vacancies or double vacancies [27].

prior_approach.content: Previous graphene work with similar-energy Ar+ in the same setup mainly produced double vacancies
prior_approach.evidence_span: In comparison to our previous work where graphene was defect-engineered using Ar+ ions at a similar energy and with the same setup [35, 36], we find that the defect-size distributions are curiously different. In the case of graphene, we primarily create double vacancies

prior_approach.content: It is usually assumed singly charged ion impacts can be modeled without explicit charge because ions neutralize before impact
prior_approach.evidence_span: it is typically assumed that singly-charged ion impacts can be modeled without taking charges into account, because prior to impact, the ion receives an electron from the sample, hence neutralizing it [61].

prior_approach.content: DFT threshold calculations found lower displacement threshold for boron than nitrogen in neutral hBN
prior_approach.evidence_span: With DFT-based molecular dynamics, the calculated displacement threshold energy in a neutral hBN lattice is lower for boron than for nitrogen (19.36 eV vs. 23.06 eV, respectively) [49].

prior_limitation.content: Electron irradiation in STEM is extremely localized.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: has the disadvantage of being extremely localized

prior_limitation.content: High-energy ion irradiation has relatively low defect-creation efficiency, especially in thin samples.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: high-energy ion irradiation efficiency for defect creation is relatively low, especially in thin specimens.

prior_limitation.content: These simulation predictions lacked experimental confirmation.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, these predictions have not been confirmed experimentally.

prior_limitation.content: Wang et al. reported an unexpectedly high intrinsic defect density.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: An unexpectedly high intrinsic defect density of 0.14 nm−2 was reported

prior_limitation.content: Exact defect identification by ADF imaging is impractical for few- and multilayer hBN because contrast differences become indistinguishable with thickness and aberrations.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: it should be noted that exact defect identification using ADF imaging for few- and multilayer hBN is beyond practical feasibility as intensity differences between boron or nitrogen dominated columns (AA′ stacking) and defects become increasingly indistinguishable with increasing thickness of hBN, which is further complicated by common residual aberrations [26].

prior_limitation.content: Those prior results were unclear because of a bimodal ion-beam energy profile and inability to resolve impurity atoms conclusively.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Although ion irradiation did yield some selectivity in the defects created, the results were unclear because of a bimodal ion-beam energy profile and, importantly, the imaging conditions failed to conclusively resolve impurity atoms in the lattice.

prior_limitation.content: Carbon-filled defects are hard to detect with the CNN because of similar contrast
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Unlike Si, it is much more difficult to detect carbon-filled defects (CB and CN ) through the CNN-assisted analysis, due to the similar atomic number of B, C and N (and therefore ADF contrast [43]).

prior_limitation.content: Post-irradiation image noise and intensity fluctuations further hinder detection of carbon substitutions
prior_limitation.evidence_span: The post-irradiation datasets were also generally more noisy and had higher intensity fluctuations in the images, which added to the difficulty in detection of these carbon substitutions

prior_limitation.content: Wang et al. did not account for electron-beam damage and chemical effects
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Since they do not take electron-beam damage at 60 kV ... and chemical effects ... into account, this could possibly explain the number of vacancies and the prevalence for B site vacancies.

rejected_alternative.content: They avoided repeatedly imaging already exposed regions to reduce beam damage
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: To minimize the number of imaging-induced defects, each dataset acquired using the semi-automated imaging tool was taken from a region that had previously not been exposed to the electron beam.

causal_claim.content: Vacancy filling by Si and C impurities significantly contributes to created defects and may hinder selective emitter creation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Moreover, we also observe that vacancy filling with Si and C impurity atoms plays a more significant role in the created defects than previously assumed, potentially posing a problem for selective creation of quantum emitters in hBN.

causal_claim.content: Defect density was high enough to confirm irradiation damage but low enough that most ions hit pristine sites only once.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This defect density is sufficiently high to confirm irradiation-related damage yet low enough that most ions encounter pristine hBN, ensuring that ions rarely impact the exact same location more than once.

causal_claim.content: Vacancy filling appears to be an uncontrollable by-product of ion irradiation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This vacancy filling appears to be an uncontrollable by-product of ion irradiation.

causal_claim.content: Because impurities mostly fill boron sites, vacancy filling cannot explain the mismatch by hiding nitrogen vacancies.
causal_claim.evidence_span: hence ruling out the possibility that the discrepancy between simulations and experiments could be explained by vacancy filling that obscures the number of nitrogen single vacancies created by the irradiation.

causal_claim.content: Ultra-low-energy noble-gas irradiation can achieve some defect selectivity in hBN despite competing impurity filling.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Overall, the results presented here show that a degree of defect selectivity can indeed be achieved in hBN with ultra-low-energy noble gas irradiation, despite a competing mechanism vacancy filling by impurity atoms.

causal_claim.content: Defect production is much more efficient with <1 keV ions than with >20 keV ions.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This also confirms that defect production is much more efficient with <1 keV ions compared to >20 keV ions

causal_claim.content: The imaging electron beam is expected to create single vacancies at a specific density
causal_claim.evidence_span: we expect 0.024 – 0.034 nm−2 single vacancies to be induced by the electron beam within the respective FOV during the imaging process

causal_claim.content: The increase in substitutional atoms suggests vacancy filling happens during or just after irradiation
causal_claim.evidence_span: Since we do not see nearly as many substitutional atoms in the pre-irradiation datasets (0.004 nm−2 compared to 0.036 nm−2 ), we believe this process occurs during and/or immediately after the irradiation but before the STEM imaging.

causal_claim.content: Charged defects likely modify the bonding environment and displacement threshold energy
causal_claim.evidence_span: the corresponding density (1 defect per ca. 4.4 nm2 ) of possibly charged defects [55] is likely to alter the bonding environment, causing a change in the displacement threshold energy.

causal_claim.content: Charged defects may also influence neutralization of approaching ions
causal_claim.evidence_span: Similarly, it may have an influence on the neutralization of the approaching charged ion

causal_claim.content: Ultra-low-energy Ar+ irradiation enables selective creation of boron single vacancies in hBN
causal_claim.evidence_span: we demonstrated that ultra-low-energy Ar+ irradiation is a suitable method for defect engineering hBN with a high selectivity for boron single vacancies.

causal_claim.content: Ion irradiation causes vacancy filling by impurity atoms such as silicon, carbon, and possibly oxygen
causal_claim.evidence_span: Our results also reveal a largely under-studied phenomenon of vacancy filling by impurity atoms (silicon, carbon, and possibly oxygen) as a result of ion irradiation

causal_claim.content: Ultra-low-energy irradiation creates defects much more efficiently than high-energy irradiation experiments
causal_claim.evidence_span: we demonstrate that ultra-low-energy ion irradiation creates defects far more efficiently than higher-energy irradiation experiments

mechanism_principle.content: Higher efficiency at lower ion energy is attributed to a larger displacement cross section.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: as would be expected from the larger displacement cross section at lower energies.

mechanism_principle.content: The intrinsic defect density may arise from unavoidable electron-beam-induced defects and defects from growth, preparation, or cleaning.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: that could be explained, at least in part, by unavoidable electron-beam-induced defects along with the possibility of intrinsic defects being present in the material either from the growth or introduced during the sample preparation or cleaning procedure.

mechanism_principle.content: Impurity-filled vacancies can make nitrogen vacancies appear overcounted, especially with carbon near double vacancies
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: these simulations indicate that nitrogen single vacancies will be overestimated if there is a significant number of C or O impurity atoms incorporated in the created defects but not recognized during the analysis.

mechanism_principle.content: Not all pre-irradiation defects came from the beam because many are too large to form during one image acquisition
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: it is unlikely that all recorded pre-irradiation defects are introduced by the electron beam, mainly because larger defects (size ≥ 3) make up ∼40% of all defects, and are unlikely to form during the acquisition of a single image

mechanism_principle.content: Defective hBN may be easier to damage than pristine hBN
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: another explanation could be that it is easier to damage a defective material than a pristine one, as reported in Ref. [49].

mechanism_principle.content: The defect creation efficiency uncertainty is large because current depends strongly on Faraday cup alignment and sample position
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The uncertainty for the defect creation efficiency is relatively large due to the measured ion-beam current being highly dependent on the exact position of the Faraday cup, which is prone to misalignment. Additionally, the position of the sample during the irradiation can vary, contributing to further uncertainty.

mechanism_principle.content: Neutralized ions may still create defects without contributing to measured current
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: There may also be cases where ions are neutralized on the way to the cup/sample but retain their kinetic energy and could thus induce defects without contributing to the current.

mechanism_principle.content: If double vacancies are created, impurity filling can convert them into apparent monoatomic defects and shift the size distribution smaller
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: vacancy filling by carbon, oxygen, and silicon atoms, as discussed earlier, could fill one (or two) of the atomic sites in a double vacancy and form a monoatomic defect that is then imaged. This would, of course, also be occurring for the larger defect sizes, resulting in the size distribution shifting towards smaller defects.

mechanism_principle.content: Graphene vacancies can migrate and agglomerate due to bond rearrangement, unlike in hBN
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: bond rearrangement in graphene allow vacancies to migrate and agglomerate, forming larger defects. Some part of the differences in the defect sizes between graphene and hBN could also be explained due to this vacancy agglomeration, since bond rearrangement is not possible in hBN [48].

mechanism_principle.content: More efficient Ar-to-N momentum transfer alone cannot explain the experiments
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Since energy transfer from Ar to N is more efficient than to B, due to momentum conservation and the higher mass of N ... this fact by itself is not sufficient to explain our experimental results.

hypothesis_statement.content: Selective creation and characterization of specific point defects in hBN is desirable.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Therefore, being able to selectively create specific types of point defects in hBN and to characterize their atomic structure would be desirable.

hypothesis_statement.content: The present work aims to improve the experimental comparison to simulations by using better-defined ion energy and improved imaging.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here, we improve on this work to make the comparison between experiments and simulations more straightforward. Specifically, we conduct singly charged argon irradiation experiments at 150 eV with a better defined ion energy and improved STEM image acquisition parameters.

hypothesis_statement.content: A different mechanism may operate in hBN than in graphene under similar irradiation.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: indicating that a different mechanism could be taking place in hBN.

hypothesis_statement.content: Impurity atoms may come from contamination patches mobilized by ions and fill nearby vacancies
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This could indicate that the impurity atoms originate from the contamination, and are mobilised by the ions which then diffuse and fill vacancies that are closest to them.

hypothesis_statement.content: Vacancy filling may make hBN defects appear smaller than those originally created
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: One explanation could be that, in the case of hBN, we might be imaging a ‘smaller’ defect than what was created by the ion irradiation.

hypothesis_statement.content: Localized charge in insulating hBN may alter thresholds and ion neutralization near impacts
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: this is not necessarily true for an insulator such as hBN, where the charge may remain localized in the vicinity of the impact point

hypothesis_statement.content: Mean-field Ehrenfest simulations may be insufficient; separate quantum-state pathways may be needed
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: it is also possible that the mean-field description of Ehrenfest simulations is insufficient to capture the bond breaking process in hBN under ion irradiation, and that the pathways associated with different quantum states during the charge transfer processes would need to be modeled separately for an accurate description.

evidence_result.content: Boron single vacancies were the main observed irradiation-induced defect, with double vacancies about half as common.
evidence_result.evidence_span: we predominantly observe boron single vacancies after ion irradiation, followed by double vacancies at half the count

evidence_result.content: Measured intrinsic pre-irradiation defect density was 0.021 nm−2, similar to literature values for CVD monolayer hBN.
evidence_result.evidence_span: We find an intrinsic, pre-irradiation defect density of 0.021 nm−2 , similar to what has been reported in literature for CVD-grown monolayer hBN [29].

evidence_result.content: After irradiation, total defect density was 0.228 nm−2 at average fluence 0.8±0.2 ions nm−2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The total defect density after irradiation was measured to be 0.228 nm−2 , for an average ion fluence of 0.8±0.2 ions nm−2 .

evidence_result.content: The most common post-irradiation defect was VB at 0.089 nm−2, followed by double vacancies at 0.042 nm−2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The most prevalent defect is the boron single vacancy (VB ) with a defect density of 0.089 nm−2 , followed by double vacancies at 0.042 nm−2 .

evidence_result.content: A large number of Si substitutions on boron sites were observed at 0.035 nm−2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: We also, unexpectedly, observe a large number of silicon atom substitutions in boron sites (SiB ) at a density of 0.035 nm−2 .

evidence_result.content: The as-prepared samples had a non-negligible defect density of 0.021 nm−2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The as-prepared samples show a non-negligible defect density of 0.021 nm−2

evidence_result.content: After irradiation the defect density was 0.228 nm−2, about ten times the pre-irradiation value, with ion-induced density 0.207 nm−2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: A defect density of 0.228 nm−2 was measured from the analysis resulting in an ion-induced defect density of 0.207 nm−2 , which is roughly ten times higher than the pre-irradiation value (0.021 nm−2 ).

evidence_result.content: Beam-induced defect estimate is comparable to the measured pre-irradiation defect density
evidence_result.evidence_span: This is comparable to the measured pre-irradiation defect density (0.021 nm−2 ) in our as-prepared hBN samples.

evidence_result.content: The twice-imaged region had a higher post-irradiation defect density than elsewhere by 0.04 nm−2
evidence_result.evidence_span: we measure a post-irradiation defect density that is higher by 0.04 nm−2 , compared to the total post-irradiation defect density elsewhere

evidence_result.content: Si substitutions overwhelmingly occupy boron vacancies rather than nitrogen vacancies
evidence_result.evidence_span: we only found 5 VN sites being filled by Si (SiN ), compared to 616 VB sites (SiB )

evidence_result.content: Si substitutions are more common near contamination regions
evidence_result.evidence_span: we observe that more SiB defects are found closer to contamination regions than away from them.

evidence_result.content: Detected carbon substitutions were rare in both pre- and post-irradiation datasets
evidence_result.evidence_span: we were able to detect 20 CN and 6 CB in the pre-irradiation datasets, and 4 CN and 6 CB in the post-irradiation datasets.

evidence_result.content: Liang et al. reported about 0.09 nm−2 defects at 30 ions nm−2, or about 0.3% probability per ion
evidence_result.evidence_span: They report a defect density of ca. 0.09 nm−2 for a fluence of 30 ions nm−2 which would correspond to a defect creation probability of around 0.3% per ion.

evidence_result.content: Liang et al. observed a defect distribution similar to this study, with boron sites more prone to vacancy formation and impurity uptake
evidence_result.evidence_span: their induced defect distribution is similar to the one in our study; also showing that B sites are more prone to vacancy formation which are then also more prone to adatom absorption/interacalants, relative to N sites.

evidence_result.content: From Byrne et al.'s data, defect creation probability is about 0.17% per ion
evidence_result.evidence_span: Extracting the ion-induced defect density from the data they report, results in a ca. 0.17% probability of creating a defect per ion.

evidence_result.content: Measured ion-induced defect creation probability is about 26±5%
evidence_result.evidence_span: With an ion fluence of 0.8±0.2 nm−2 and an ion-induced defect density of 0.207 nm−2 , we show a defect-creation probability of about 26±5%.

evidence_result.content: Ignoring vacancy filling, experiments show about a 6:1 ratio of boron to nitrogen single vacancies and about 3:1 single to double vacancies
evidence_result.evidence_span: Ignoring vacancy filling, the resulting defect distribution shows a ca. 6:1 ratio of B:N single vacancies and a roughly 3:1 ratio of single to double vacancies.

evidence_result.content: Including ion charge in Ehrenfest simulations still gave nearly equal B and N displacement probabilities
evidence_result.evidence_span: Even when the charge of the impinging ion was included in Ehrenfest simulations described above, the results showed approximately equal probability for displacing either boron or nitrogen atoms from hBN following an impact by a 150 eV Ar+ ion.

evidence_result.content: Pre-irradiation defect density was 0.021 nm−2 and beam damage was estimated at 0.024–0.034 nm−2 within the field of view
evidence_result.evidence_span: The pre-irradiation defect density in the as-prepared and cleaned samples was found to be 0.021 nm−2 which also includes electron-beam damage, estimated to induce 0.024 – 0.034 nm−2 single vacancies within the FOV during semi-automated imaging of the samples.

evidence_result.content: After irradiation, defect density was 0.228 nm−2, mainly monoatomic defects with preference for boron vacancies
evidence_result.evidence_span: After irradiation, we measured a defect density of 0.228 nm−2 of primarily monoatomic defects with a preference for VB .

constraint.content: Atomic-resolution analysis must account for electron-beam damage and beam-assisted chemical etching.
constraint.evidence_span: taking into account the effect of electron-beam damage [23] and beam-assisted chemical etching [24]

constraint.content: Imaging analysis must account for beam-induced defects
constraint.evidence_span: this defect needs to be correctly taken into account.

constraint.content: Further cleaning is limited by defects and metal contamination introduced during growth
constraint.evidence_span: Achieving cleaner samples beyond this, is limited by the defects and metal contamination that is most likely introduced during the growth of the material [34].

constraint.content: Irradiation fluence had to be high enough to separate ion-induced from intrinsic defects but low enough to avoid hitting existing defects
constraint.evidence_span: The ion irradiation fluence was chosen to be high enough to separate the irradiation-induced defects from the intrinsic ones, but sufficiently low to mostly avoid ions impinging on already defective sites.

constraint.content: Electron-beam characterization itself can induce defects, so interpretation must be careful
constraint.evidence_span: careful interpretation is needed when using electron-beam characterisation, as the measurement process itself can induce defects [23, 47–49].

contradiction.content: Experiment predominantly found boron single vacancies rather than the simulated dominant nitrogen vacancies.
contradiction.evidence_span: Contrary to what analytical potential molecular dynamics simulations have predicted, we predominantly observe boron single vacancies after ion irradiation, followed by double vacancies at half the count.

contradiction.content: Observed defect distributions did not match simulation predictions.
contradiction.evidence_span: Interestingly, these results do not align with the predicted defect distributions reported by the simulation studies [27, 28].

contradiction.content: Unlike earlier reports with few impurity substitutions, post-irradiation impurities here mostly occupy boron sites.
contradiction.evidence_span: Contrary to the limited number of impurity atom substitutions reported in Refs. [31, 32], these post-irradiation impurity atoms predominantly occupy boron sites

contradiction.content: Their simulations found no significant difference between ejection of B and N atoms, contrary to experiment but consistent with prior simulations.
contradiction.evidence_span: Contrary to our experimental results, but in agreement with other simulation studies [27, 28], we find no significant difference in the ejection of B or N atoms from the lattice

contradiction.content: Observed defect pattern is not explained by the simulations
contradiction.evidence_span: Since we experimentally observe more boron single vacancies and also more impurity atom filling of boron sites, the simulations are unable to fully capture the defect creation dynamics.

contradiction.content: The extra defects in the repeatedly imaged region exceed the estimated beam-induced amount
contradiction.evidence_span: This difference is two to three times larger than the estimate for electron-beam-induced defects

contradiction.content: The experimental results clearly contradict analytical-potential MD predictions
contradiction.evidence_span: Our experimental results are, however, in clear contradiction with theoretical studies based on analytical-potential molecular-dynamics simulations

contradiction.content: Despite similar knock-on expectations, hBN shows the opposite trend from graphene, with many more monoatomic than double vacancies
contradiction.evidence_span: Assuming the same knock-on type of irradiation damage (and displacement cross-sections) for both materials, one would expect a similar defect size to be created in both cases. However, we find the opposite in hBN where we have ca. 3.4 times more monoatomic defects than double vacancies.

contradiction.content: Results challenge prior calculations predicting similar VB/VN rates or predominance of VN and VBN
contradiction.evidence_span: Our results challenge earlier computational work predicting either similar formation probabilities for VN and VB and a higher probability for VBN [28], or a predominance for VN over VB and VBN under Ar irradiation at similar energies [27].

contradiction.content: Predominance of boron vacancies is surprising given both present and prior high-energy observations
contradiction.evidence_span: Surprisingly, the predominance of VB was not only experimentally shown here, but has also been reported for much higher ion energies [25] and in the case of intrinsic defects [30].

contradiction.content: hBN irradiation behavior is much more complex than graphene, where double vacancies dominate and vacancy filling is less important
contradiction.evidence_span: We also show that the irradiation results in hBN are much more complex than in graphene [35, 36], where double vacancies dominate and vacancy filling by impurity atoms does not play as big of a role.

problem_motivation.content: A central challenge in hBN defect engineering is the lack of a satisfactory direct correlation between specific defect structures/creation mechanisms and their quantum emission spectra; therefore, controlling defect creation is required to conclusively link particular defects to their optical properties.
evidence_spans: so far no satisfactory direct correlation between the defect structures and quantum emission properties has been established
but in order to conclusively correlate specific defects to their spectra, having control over the defect creation mechanism is required

problem_motivation.content: For large-scale applications, more effective methods to generate defects are needed.
evidence_spans: For large-scale applications, a method to generate defects more effectively would be necessary.

problem_motivation.content: It remains unclear whether electron-irradiation-related effects also play a role in ultra-low-energy singly charged ion irradiation of hBN, highlighting the need for further experimental and computational study of defect-engineering mechanisms.
evidence_spans: Whether these effects play a role also for ultra-low-energy singly-charged ion irradiation of hBN remains unclear.
more research is needed both experimentally and computationally to fully understand the mechanisms involved in the defect-engineering of hBN.

prior_approach.content: Prior work has used multiple irradiation-based approaches to create or study defects/quantum emitters in hBN, including electron irradiation in STEM, high-energy ion irradiation, lasers, ions, neutrons, and electrons.

prior_approach.content: Prior simulations suggested low-energy noble-gas ion irradiation should be highly efficient and most selective below 200 eV, with nitrogen single vacancies expected to dominate for projectile species heavier than Ne.
evidence_spans: Analytical potential molecular dynamics simulations have shown that low-energy noble-gas ions should have high defect creation efficiencies.

prior_approach.content: One prior theory study (Lehtinen et al.) predicted that ~100 eV Ar ions create defects with high probability: about 0.8 defects per ion, or a 75–80% defect-creation chance, with similar probabilities for boron and nitrogen single vacancies and a higher probability for double vacancies.

it was found, depending on the potential used, that an impinging Ar ion (≈ 100 eV) has a 75–80% chance to create a defect with the probability for creating a boron or nitrogen single vacancy being 17–20% each and about 40% for a double vacancy [28].

prior_approach.content: Another prior theory study (Ghaderzadeh et al.) predicted substantially lower defect yield for Ar irradiation, about 0.2 defects per 150 eV Ar ion at low fluence, and a defect distribution dominated by nitrogen vacancies over double vacancies and boron vacancies.

prior_approach.content: Prior electron-irradiation work found boron to be more easily displaced than nitrogen in hBN: experiments at intermediate electron energies (60–100 keV) preferentially displaced boron, electron irradiation in low-pressure oxygen preferentially removed boron from pore edges, and DFT threshold calculations also gave a lower displacement threshold for boron than for nitrogen in neutral hBN.
evidence_spans: For electron irradiation, it was experimentally shown that intermediate electron energies (60–100 keV) are more likely to displace boron than nitrogen [23].
Electron irradiation in a low-pressure oxygen atmosphere has also been shown to result in preferential removal of boron, at least from pore edges [24], often leading to nitrogen-terminated pores.
With DFT-based molecular dynamics, the calculated displacement threshold energy in a neutral hBN lattice is lower for boron than for nitrogen (19.36 eV vs. 23.06 eV, respectively) [49].
